Oddly enough, I have Dunlop Enasave tyres on my Nissan LEAF which are technically low grip tyres but the combination of stability control and traction control, plus the very low centre of gravity caused by the batteries means the car actually handles really well. Tyre pressures are much higher than for any other car I've had (about 40psi) and if I let the pressures go down the car is significantly less happy at motorway speeds but overall the grip is perfectly good even in the wet. There's definitely a market for low rolling resistance tyres, but that doesn't mean you're driving around on tyres that have no grip since the tyres are built for multiple driving conditions. You can get amazing grip with slicks, or none at all with the same tyre in the wet. I don't think government should stop people buying high grip tyres for specific conditions (e.g. snow tyres) but all tyres are a compromise and you buy them for most conditions but running snow tyres in summer is a really bad idea. Low rolling resistance tyres are just another member of the range and they do make a difference to fuel (or energy) economy.
